title: Rooted
subtitle: A discipleship path for His Place
translation: Scripture quotations are from the King James Version

intro.theme_text: As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him: Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving.
about: Rooted is a twelve session path for His Place members who want to grow deeper in Christ. It isn't a membership requirement or a test. It's a guided way to build the habits and convictions that keep a believer strong for the long haul.

Each session has a short reading for the week, key Scriptures, teaching, questions to think through, a memory verse, and practical activities. Plan on one session a week. Work through it with the leader who invited you, or a mentor they connect you with, and meet to talk about what you're learning.
Be honest in your answers. Your mentor and our pastors can see what you write, and that's the point. Discipleship happens in relationship, not alone.
flow: Know the gospel that saved you and who you are in Christ (sessions 1 and 2).
Build daily habits of abiding, Scripture, and prayer (sessions 3 through 5).
Walk in the Spirit and fight sin with grace and with others beside you (sessions 6 through 8).
Stand firm in trials, share Christ, serve, and make disciples (sessions 9 through 12).

blocks.text: The gospel isn't just how you got in. It's the good news you live from every day.
This week, read Romans 3 through 5.
Key Scripture

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Teaching

The word gospel means good news, and it's news about what God has done, not advice about what we should do. Paul summarizes it plainly: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, He was buried, and He rose again the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Everything in the Christian life grows out of that announcement.

Scripture is honest about our condition. All have sinned and come short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Sin isn't just breaking rules. It's turning from the God who made us, and it leaves us guilty and unable to fix ourselves. That's why salvation has to be by grace, a gift we don't earn, received through faith, which is trusting Christ rather than ourselves.

Second Corinthians 5:21 shows the great exchange. Jesus, who never sinned, took our sin on Himself at the cross, and those who trust Him receive His righteousness. Romans 5:1 calls this being justified: God declares us right with Him because of what Christ did. The result is peace with God, not a truce we have to keep earning.

Grace doesn't make obedience unimportant. Ephesians 2:10 says we're God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works. We don't work to be saved. Saved people work because grace has changed them. When you fail, the gospel doesn't change. Run back to it, not away from God.

Your identity comes from Christ, not from your past, your failures, or other people's opinions.
This week, read Ephesians 1 and 2, Romans 8.
Key Scripture

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.

For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: And if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Teaching

When someone trusts Christ, Scripture says they are united with Him. Paul can say, I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me (Galatians 2:20). The old life that sin defined has died, and a new life has begun that's joined to Jesus.

One of the richest pictures of this is adoption. Romans 8:15-17 says believers have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. You aren't a hired hand trying to stay on God's good side. You're a son or daughter, and an heir with Christ. Many of us carry wounds from earthly fathers, so this truth may take time to sink in. It's still true.

First Peter 2:9 describes God's people as a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people. The word peculiar here means a people belonging to God. Your worth is settled by whose you are.

Knowing who you are in Christ doesn't make you proud. It makes you secure. Secure people can admit their faults, take correction, serve without needing credit, and love people who don't love them back. Much of our sin grows from trying to find identity somewhere other than Christ.

Fruitfulness doesn't come from trying harder. It comes from staying connected to Christ.
This week, read John 14 and 15.
Key Scripture

Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.

And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.
Teaching

Jesus gave His disciples a simple picture the night before the cross. He is the vine, and we are the branches. A branch doesn't strain to produce grapes. It stays connected, and the life of the vine flows through it. Without me ye can do nothing, Jesus said (John 15:5).

Abiding means remaining in close, ongoing relationship with Jesus: trusting Him, listening to His word, talking with Him, and obeying Him. It's not a feeling you wait for. It's a way of living that's built through daily habits.

Jesus Himself made time alone with the Father. Mark 1:35 says that rising up a great while before day, He went out into a solitary place and prayed. If the Son of God set aside time with His Father, we certainly need it too.

Busyness is one of the biggest enemies of abiding. Martha was serving Jesus and got so distracted she missed Him, while Mary sat at His feet (Luke 10:41-42). Serving matters, but it was never meant to replace time with Him. A daily quiet time isn't a religious chore. It's where the branch stays connected to the vine.

lessons.title: Feeding on the Word
lessons.reading: the Gospel of Mark, a few chapters a day

blocks.text: Scripture is God's voice to His people. It's how we learn who He is and how to live.
This week, read the Gospel of Mark, a few chapters a day.
Key Scripture

All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Teaching

Paul told Timothy that all scripture is given by inspiration of God (2 Timothy 3:16). The idea is that Scripture is breathed out by God. That's why it carries His authority and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.

God gave His Word for a purpose: that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:17). The word perfect here means complete or fully equipped. The Bible isn't meant to sit on a shelf. It's meant to equip you for the life God has called you to.

A simple way to study any passage is to ask three questions. Observe: What does it say? Interpret: What did it mean to the people who first heard it, and what does it show us about God? Apply: What do I need to believe, change, or do because of it? Read slowly. Read the verses around a passage so you don't pull it out of context.

James warns against being hearers only, deceiving your own selves (James 1:22). The goal of Bible reading isn't information. It's transformation. A few verses read carefully and obeyed will change you more than many chapters skimmed and forgotten.

Prayer is a child talking with a loving Father, not a performance or a wish list.
This week, read Matthew 6 and 7, Psalm 145.
Key Scripture

After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
Teaching

When the disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray, He gave them a model that begins with Our Father (Matthew 6:9). Prayer starts with relationship. Because of Christ, we come to God as children, not strangers.

The Lord's Prayer puts God first: His name, His kingdom, His will. Then it brings our needs: daily bread, forgiveness, and protection from temptation and evil. One helpful pattern that follows this shape is ACTS: Adoration, praising God for who He is; Confession, owning our sin; Thanksgiving, thanking Him for what He's done; and Supplication, asking for our needs and the needs of others.

Philippians 4:6-7 tells us to be careful for nothing, meaning don't be anxious about anything, but bring everything to God by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving. The promise isn't that we'll always get what we ask. It's that the peace of God will keep our hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.

Hebrews 4:16 invites us to come boldly unto the throne of grace. We can be bold because Jesus is our great High Priest who understands our weakness. Prayer isn't about fancy words. Honest, simple, persistent prayer pleases the Father.

The Holy Spirit lives in every believer to make us like Jesus and empower us to serve.
This week, read John 14 through 16, Galatians 5.
Key Scripture

And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.
This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.
Teaching

Jesus promised His followers another Comforter who would abide with them for ever, the Spirit of truth (John 14:16-17). The Holy Spirit is not a force or a feeling. He is God, the third Person of the Trinity, and He lives in every believer. Romans 8:9 says that if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.

The Spirit teaches and reminds us of what Jesus said, guides us into truth, convicts us of sin, comforts us, helps us pray, and gives us power to be witnesses (John 14:26, John 16:8 and 13, Romans 8:26, Acts 1:8). He also gives each believer gifts to serve others, given for the good of the whole church (1 Corinthians 12:7).

Galatians 5:16 says, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. Walking in the Spirit means depending on Him moment by moment: listening, yielding, and obeying. The flesh, our sinful nature, still pulls at us, but the Spirit is stronger.

The evidence of the Spirit's work isn't mainly dramatic moments. It's fruit: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, and temperance (Galatians 5:22-23). Fruit grows slowly and steadily. Look for it over months and years, not days.

God's grace forgives our sin and trains us to say no to it.
This week, read Romans 6 through 8.
Key Scripture

Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof. Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin: but yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Teaching

Romans 6 teaches that believers have died to sin's rule through union with Christ. We are told to reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God (Romans 6:11). Reckon means count it as true. Sin is no longer your master, even when it still tempts you.

Grace is not a license to sin. Titus 2:11-12 says the grace of God that brings salvation teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world. The same grace that forgives also trains.

First Corinthians 10:13 gives a promise for every temptation. No temptation is unique to you, God is faithful, and He will with the temptation also make a way to escape. Part of fighting sin is planning ahead: knowing your weak spots, avoiding situations that feed them, and taking the way out when it shows up.

When we do sin, the answer isn't to hide. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Confession to God brings forgiveness. Confession to a trusted believer brings help and healing (James 5:16). Sin grows in secret and weakens in the light.

No believer is meant to follow Jesus alone. We grow together in the body of Christ.
This week, read Acts 2, 1 Corinthians 12, Hebrews 10.
Key Scripture
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.

Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Teaching

From the very beginning, believers gathered. Acts 2:42 says they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. Teaching, fellowship, sharing life, and prayer were the heartbeat of the early church.

Paul describes the church as a body with many members (1 Corinthians 12:12-27). Every part matters, and every part needs the others. A believer who drifts from the body is like a hand cut off from the arm. It can't thrive alone.

Hebrews 10:24-25 tells us to consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works, and not to forsake the assembling of ourselves together. That's why being an active part of a local church matters so much. Online sermons, podcasts, and Christian friends are good gifts, but they aren't a substitute for a church family, pastors, and the baptism and Lord's Supper that Christ gave His church.

Galatians 6:1-2 shows what a church family looks like when someone falls. Those who are spiritual restore such an one in the spirit of meekness, and we bear one another's burdens. Real fellowship is more than sitting in the same room on Sunday. It's speaking the truth in love and carrying each other's loads.

God uses hard seasons to grow faith that lasts, and He never wastes our pain.
This week, read James 1, 2 Corinthians 4, 1 Peter 1.
Key Scripture

My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.

And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.

For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory; While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Teaching

Jesus never promised His followers an easy road. He said, In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world (John 16:33). Trials aren't a sign that God has abandoned you.

James 1:2-4 tells us to count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations, meaning trials, because the trying of our faith works patience. That doesn't mean we pretend pain feels good. It means we trust God is doing something in the pain: building endurance and maturity.

Romans 5:3-5 traces the same path. Tribulation works patience, patience experience, which means proven character, and experience hope. That hope doesn't disappoint, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost.

Paul faced beatings, shipwrecks, and prison, yet he called his troubles a light affliction, which is but for a moment, compared to the eternal weight of glory ahead (2 Corinthians 4:17). The key is where we look. We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. Lament is allowed. The Psalms are full of honest grief. But we grieve with hope.

Every believer is called to be a witness, ready to tell what Jesus has done.
This week, read Acts 1 through 4.
Key Scripture

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:
Teaching

Before He ascended, Jesus told His followers, ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me (Acts 1:8). A witness simply tells what they have seen and know. You don't have to be a preacher to be a witness.

Peter tells us to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3:15). Ready means prepared. Meekness and fear mean gentleness and respect. Bold doesn't mean pushy.

The heart of the message is the gospel: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Your story matters because it shows the gospel at work in a real life, but your story should always point to Jesus, not to you.

Results belong to God. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6). Our job is to be faithful and clear. The Holy Spirit is the one who opens hearts. That takes pressure off and puts courage in.

Jesus came to serve, and He calls us to use everything we've been given for others.
This week, read Mark 10, Philippians 2, John 13.
Key Scripture
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
Teaching

James and John asked Jesus for the best seats in His kingdom. Jesus answered that greatness in His kingdom looks completely different: the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

Philippians 2:3-5 calls us to esteem others better than ourselves and to look on the things of others, then says, Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. The verses that follow describe Jesus humbling Himself all the way to the cross. Christian service flows from the humility of Christ.

Everything we have is on loan from God: time, money, abilities, cars, homes, and spiritual gifts. First Peter 4:10 says that as every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. A steward manages what belongs to someone else.

Jesus said that faithfulness in small things matters to God (Luke 16:10), and He will one day say to faithful servants, Well done (Matthew 25:21). Service done for His glory, even when nobody notices, is never wasted.

The goal of discipleship is not just to grow, but to help someone else grow too.
This week, read Matthew 28, 2 Timothy 2, 1 Thessalonians 2.
Key Scripture

And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
So being affectionately desirous of you, we were willing to have imparted unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us.
Teaching

Jesus' final command before He ascended was clear. All power is given unto Him, so go and teach all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe all things He commanded (Matthew 28:18-20). The goal isn't just converts. It's disciples who follow and obey Jesus. And He promised, lo, I am with you alway.

Paul showed how disciples multiply: the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). That's four generations in one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others.

Discipleship is relational. Paul told the Thessalonians that he was willing to share not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were dear unto us (1 Thessalonians 2:8). You don't need to have all the answers to disciple someone. You need to love them, walk with them, open the Word together, and point them to Jesus.

You've spent twelve sessions growing. Now look around. Who is a step or two behind you? A new believer, someone new at His Place, a young person, a family member? The best way to keep growing is to help someone else grow.
